name: Beth Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time, Beth. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to companies, unions, parties or government. What you say here is confidential. Could you tell me what a normal working day is like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now it's potato harvest, so it's long. I'm third generation on this place, Long Lane Farm, about 150 hectares: beef cattle, hay, and potatoes we sell to a crisp factory on contract. I've one full-time man, Gordon, and in autumn eight or nine seasonal pickers and graders. Matt, my husband, is an electrician, so he's out on jobs and I'm the one on the harvester.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you feel about new technology on the farm?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I don't go looking for it. We've a harvester that's twelve years old and I know every noise it makes. My dad bought one gadget a year and sold half of them at the farm sale, so I learned to wait. I've never used one of those AI chat things and I don't see why I'd start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say well, there you go, lots of fuss about nothing. Probably at the market, leaning on a pen with the other beef men. Nobody would be very surprised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be quite pleased. I've watched people spend money on things that didn't pay. This way I don't have to decide anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on, same as always. Get the potatoes in, sell the store cattle in spring, pay the mortgage on the new barn. If the crisp factory used AI to plan their lorries, that's up to them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleased not to be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd miss out on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the grading. The crisp factory knocks us down for bruised potatoes and it's always an argument. If a machine could stop the factory cheating me on bruising, I'd buy that one tomorrow. But that's about the only thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Gordon say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon would say nothing, he never does. He'd light a cigarette and go back to the cattle. He's been here nineteen years.

S0.say: I'd say it was a lot of fuss about nothing, probably at the market with the other beef farmers. Nobody there would be very surprised.
S0.think: Privately I'd be quite pleased, because I've watched people waste money on things that didn't pay. It means I don't have to decide anything.
S0.do: Carries on as always: gets the potatoes in, sells the store cattle in spring and keeps paying the mortgage on the new barn. Leaves any AI use to the crisp factory.
S0.feel: Calm and pleased not to be pushed.
S0.quote: If a machine could stop the factory cheating me on bruising, I'd buy that one tomorrow.
S0.fieldNote: Beth learned caution from watching her father buy gadgets that didn't pay off. The one thing she'd want from technology is a fair grade on bruised potatoes, which shows her real grievance is with the factory. Gordon, her long-time worker, is part of the furniture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's see what actually works before anyone panics. Some of it will be useful, most of it won't. That's what I'd say at the farmers' discussion group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the potato side worries me. Picking and grading is exactly what a machine with a camera would take over, and the crisp factory would want it. The beef I'm not worried about, cattle are cattle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait. I'd let the big potato growers in the county try the new graders first and see what they cost. If the factory made it a condition of the contract, I'd hire it in for the season rather than buy it. I'd keep the cash where it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a contract renewal you're not sure about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your seasonal pickers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the hard part. Some of them have come back to us for ten years, the Kowalski brothers especially. If a camera grades the potatoes, the Kowalskis don't come back in September, and I'd miss them more than I'd admit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd hire rather than buy. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if it's rubbish I can send it back. You can't send a loan back. Matt says I'm too careful, and he's probably right, but we've never been in trouble.

S1.say: I'd say let's see what actually works before anyone panics, because some of it will be useful and most of it won't. I'd say that at the farmers' discussion group.
S1.think: Privately the potato side worries me, because picking and grading is exactly what a camera-guided machine would take over. The beef cattle I'm not worried about.
S1.do: Waits for the big potato growers in the county to try the new graders first. If the crisp factory makes it a condition of the contract, hires the machine in for the season instead of buying, and keeps the cash where it is.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like waiting on a contract renewal.
S1.quote: If a camera grades the potatoes, the Kowalskis don't come back in September, and I'd miss them more than I'd admit.
S1.fieldNote: Beth splits her farm in two: beef she sees as safe, potatoes as exposed. Her instinct is to hire rather than buy so she can back out. She shows real feeling for the seasonal pickers who've come for years, which she says she'd never admit in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready, the government isn't, the banks aren't, and they should slow it down. I'd not blame one side, I'd say they've all been asleep. I'd say it at the market and in the discussion group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it frightens me. I've got land and savings, so we wouldn't starve, but if a robot can run a farm then big companies will want to run them, and the crisp factory will grow its own potatoes. I'm not someone who changes quickly, and two years is quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on the farm, no new kit, nothing. I'd get the barn mortgage down as fast as I could. I'd talk to Matt about whether we rent the land out to whoever's got the robots and keep the cattle as a smaller thing. Honestly, I think I'd freeze for the first few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at three, which I never am except at calving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd freeze. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Doing the same jobs every morning and not opening the post. Matt would end up making the calls. I'd be feeding cattle by hand while somebody else's robot dug my potatoes on rented ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Lily and Sam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lily's twelve, she'd notice I was off. I'd tell them we've got the land and that's not going anywhere. I'd want to believe it myself.

S2.say: I'd say nobody is ready, not the government or the banks, and they should slow it down. I wouldn't blame one side; I'd say they've all been asleep.
S2.think: Privately it frightens me: we have land and savings, but big companies would run robot farms and the crisp factory might grow its own potatoes. I don't change quickly, and two years is quick.
S2.do: Stops all spending on the farm and pays the barn mortgage down as fast as she can. Talks with Matt about renting the land to an operator with robots and keeping a smaller herd, though she expects to freeze for the first few months.
S2.feel: Alarmed and awake at three in the morning, which only usually happens at calving.
S2.quote: I'd be feeding cattle by hand while somebody else's robot dug my potatoes on rented ground.
S2.fieldNote: Beth is frank that her nature is to freeze, and that Matt would end up making the calls. She has a strong asset base but doesn't feel protected, because the threat is to the whole way of farming. Her image of hand-feeding cattle while someone else's robot works her land is striking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years isn't long for a farm, it's one rotation and a bit. I'd say the government should help family farms through it, and stop the big firms buying up land cheap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years helps a bit. I'd have time to watch what others do and not make a fool of myself. But I know me, I'd still leave it too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay off the barn in the first two years. I'd stop growing potatoes before the contract went bad, maybe year three, and put that ground into grass for more cattle. And I'd sit Lily down about what she wants to study, because she'd be leaving school about when it hits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but not losing sleep yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave it too late. What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing someone I trust do it and not regret it. If old Hamish Grant puts a robot on his potatoes and still smiles at the market, I'll know it's real. He's the most careful man I know, worse than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving to more cattle, is that because you think cattle are safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, but I don't really know. A robot can't calve a heifer, can it? I'd be guessing.

S3.say: I'd say five years isn't long on a farm, just one crop rotation and a bit. I'd say the government should help family farms through it and stop big firms buying land cheap.
S3.think: Privately five years helps a bit, as I'd have time to watch others. But I know I'd still probably leave it too late.
S3.do: Pays off the barn mortgage in the first two years and stops growing potatoes around year three, moving that ground to grass for more cattle. Talks with Lily about what she'll study, since she'd be leaving school about when AGI arrives.
S3.feel: Anxious but not losing sleep yet.
S3.quote: If old Hamish Grant puts a robot on his potatoes and still smiles at the market, I'll know it's real.
S3.fieldNote: Beth's move to more cattle is based on a guess that livestock is safer, and she admits she doesn't really know. She'd only move once a trusted, careful neighbour does. The extra time mostly changes the order of her decisions, not her caution.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time, so let's not get silly about it. Plan it like you'd plan a succession, step by step. I'd say farmers should look after their land and not sell it in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's the one I can live with. I'd be 53. I could pay everything off, keep the land and decide calmly what to do with it. I'd still be the last on the road to buy a robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as I am for the first five years, pay off the barn, and keep saving. Somewhere around year five I'd start renting some ground to a younger farmer with the kit. I'd make sure Lily and Sam had money for college whatever they chose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in the normal way, like weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever learn to use the new tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, if I'm honest. Matt might, he's the electrician. I'll leave the robots to Matt and the cows to me, and we'll meet at the kitchen table.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Gordon in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gordon would be 67 by then, so he'd retire whatever happened. I'd want to see him right. He's been here longer than my kids.

S4.say: I'd say there's time, so let's plan it step by step like a farm succession. I'd tell farmers to look after their land and not sell it in a hurry.
S4.think: Privately it's the one I can live with: at 53 I could pay everything off, keep the land and decide calmly. I'd still be the last on the road to buy a robot.
S4.do: Keeps farming as she is for about five years, clears the barn mortgage and keeps saving. Around year five starts renting some ground to a younger farmer with the robots, and puts money aside for Lily and Sam's college.
S4.feel: Uneasy in an everyday way, like weather.
S4.quote: I'll leave the robots to Matt and the cows to me, and we'll meet at the kitchen table.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Beth relaxes into her usual plan: keep the land, pay down debt and let others take the risks. She sees Matt, the electrician, as the one who'd handle the machines. She wants to look after Gordon, who'll retire anyway.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'm slow and I know it. What would help is someone straight, a farm adviser who isn't selling anything, telling me what actually works. And rules so the big firms can't buy up land for nothing when everyone's panicking.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Not really. Maybe what it means for the market, the auction. That's where you see your neighbours every week. If that goes, it's not just jobs, it's the whole week gone.

headlineQuote: My dad bought one gadget a year and sold half of them at the farm sale, so I learned to wait.
portrait: Beth Ziegler is 43 and farms Long Lane, a third-generation beef, hay and potato farm, with one full-time worker and seasonal pickers. She's never used an AI tool and learned caution from watching her father waste money on gadgets. She's pragmatic and doesn't blame one side, preferring to wait, watch trusted neighbours and hire rather than buy. She's calm when AI fizzles, alarmed by AGI in two years because she knows she'd freeze, and comfortable with ten years, which gives her time to keep the land and decide slowly.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, because she's slow to change and knows it.
whatWouldHelp: An honest farm adviser who isn't selling anything, and rules to stop big firms buying up land cheap when farmers are panicking.
